Description: Old Seattle that’s still here. The colored pins are businesses open to the public that started 50+ years ago (before about November 1976), each on the City of Seattle’s active business license list. Small gray dots are places on the National Register of Historic Places that still exist: buildings, historic districts, bridges, parks, ships and sites. For businesses the year is when they were founded; for Register places it is when they were added to the Register, not when they were built. Zoomed out, each neighborhood shows how many of the places shown fall inside it (City of Seattle Neighborhood Map Atlas boundaries).

Seattle Municipal Street Railway streetcar and cable car routes from the railway's own list, “Streetcar routes – April 1st, 1931,” close to the network's greatest extent. Each route is drawn outbound along today's streets, so stretches where streets have since changed are approximate. Click a line or pick a route to see its 1931 streets. Not drawn: the Seahurst shuttle (4s) from White Center to Lake Burien, whose streets the list doesn't give.

Steamer runs and ports of call from a 1908 Seattle Post-Intelligencer map of the Puget Sound “Mosquito Fleet,” with names checked against the paper’s list of 195 ports of call. The map is a diagram without a legend, so these runs are a best-effort reading of its lines. Each run is drawn over open water along today’s shorelines, keeping well offshore except in narrow channels; these are not recorded courses. Freight-only lines aren’t shown. Ports named in the paper’s list but not on its map are shown as “list only”: located from USGS place names and docks in OpenStreetMap where possible, with a follow-up note where the landing still needs checking. Lake Washington landings and crossings come from a 1909 Anderson Steamboat Co. map, with wharf positions checked on Kroll’s 1912 Atlas of King County; the lake was lowered about 9 feet in 1916, so those landings sit a little inland of today’s shore.
